newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH CPI SEEN QUICKER AFTER CROWN CRISIS-ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: CZECH CPI SEEN QUICKER AFTER CROWN CRISIS-ANALYSTS.

text.p: The downtrend of Czech inflation (CPI) should end in June, though economists unsure of the effect a major weakening of the crown would have on the data, a Reuter survey of economists showed on Monday.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) is scheduled to release June CPI data on Tuesday at 0700 GMT, and most economists forecast an increase of about 0.9 percent month-on-month, up from 0.1 percent in May.
Since December the year-on-year rate has steadily dropped from 8.6 percent to a record low of 6.3 percent in May.
But the survey showed that a 0.9 percent month-on-month figure would put the year-on-year rate for June at about 6.4 percent.

Economists said a crisis in the crown currency at the end of May and beginning of June could also have an effect on the inflation figures, although the extent of the influence is difficult to predict.
"I expect inflation to rise a little bit compared to the previous month due to seasonal changes and because of the weakening of the crown," said Jiri Krovak, chief economist at WoodCommerz in Prague.

"But it is difficult because there is no emperical evidence that inflation will be affected by the exchange rate...It's just a feeling this time, especially because of the change in the exchange rate regime that the weakening of the currency should be reflected even in inflation."
The Czech crown came under a heavy downward pressure at the end of May as speculators targeted the currency as overvalued, and the ruling coalition government teetered near a possible collapse.
The CNB was eventually forced on May 27 to float the currency and abandon its 15 percent fluctuation band within which it would fix the currency against a mark/dollar peg.

"It's tough to say what the effect of the currency fluctuation will be, but if food prices -- a major component of the inflation basket -- hold steady, it may not be a major jump," said Boris Gomez, an analyst at ING Barings in Prague.
In June 1996, foodstuffs rose 1.1 percent, year-on-year, and were the main factor behind a 0.8 percent month-on-month rise in inflation, which put the year-on-year rate at 8.4 percent.
WoodCommerz's Krovak also pointed to historical evidence that shows Czech inflation usually rises during periods of a weaker deutschemark.
"The most decisive influence on inflation so far has been the cross rate between the dollar and the deutschemark -- the stronger the dollar the higher the inflation in this country," he said.
